headline: California raid finds 235,661 lb of marijuana at Chico 'hemp' site
dek: Butte County detectives arrested 62 people on 17 November at Chico warehouses that officials say were processing marijuana under the guise of hemp.
key_points: The Butte County Sheriff's Office says it found about 235,661 pounds of marijuana in industrial warehouses on Contractors Lane in Chico on 17 November.
All 62 people found at the site were arrested and booked into the Butte County Jail; their names and charges have not been made public.
Officials say the site presented itself as a hemp processor and that testing showed the material was marijuana, not hemp.
The sheriff's $282.8 million valuation works out to $1,200 a pound, and the haul equals more than 1% of estimated yearly legal US sales by weight.
body: Detectives in Butte County, California, say they have shut down a marijuana processing operation that was presenting itself as a hemp business. The Butte County Sheriff's Office said it served a search warrant on Tuesday 17 November at large industrial warehouses on Contractors Lane in Chico and found about 235,661 pounds of marijuana in various stages of processing.

Sixty-two people were at the warehouses. All 62 were arrested and booked into the Butte County Jail the same day, according to the sheriff's account, which was published by the California Statewide Law Enforcement Association and reported by local station KRCR on 19 November. The sheriff's office put the street value at approximately $282,793,200 and said the investigation is continuing.
## What officials say happened

The case began earlier in 2026, when the sheriff's Special Enforcement Unit started assisting the federal Bureau of Land Management with a marijuana investigation. In November, detectives obtained a warrant for the Chico warehouses. The sheriff's account says they had found evidence that large quantities of marijuana were being processed there under the guise of hemp processing.

The warrant was served by sheriff's detectives with two detectives from the Butte Interagency Narcotics Task Force, two Bureau of Land Management agents and one detective from the California Department of Cannabis Control. Testing confirmed the material was marijuana, not hemp, the sheriff's office said. It took detectives three days to process the evidence and remove the product.

KRCR reported that those arrested ranged in age from 19 to 83 and that more than half were listed as being from Yuba City. No names or charges have been released in the reporting we reviewed. These are allegations by law enforcement; nobody has been convicted of anything.
## How big 235,661 pounds is
The number is large enough to need a yardstick. It is about 118 short tons, or roughly 107 tonnes.

Compare it with the legal market. Economist Beau Whitney told a Washington summit on 18 November that legal US cannabis sales amount to an estimated 15 million to 20 million pounds a year. On that basis, the Chico seizure equals between 1.2% and 1.6% of a full year of legal sales across the whole country, found in one cluster of buildings.
Or compare it with Europe. As we reported on 18 November, Germany imported 201 tonnes of medical cannabis in all of 2025. The Chico haul is a little over half of that.

One caution on the weight, which is ours: officials describe the marijuana as being in various stages of processing. The release does not say how much was dried, trimmed flower and how much was wet or untrimmed plant material, which weighs far more than the finished product. The figure should be read as gross material seized, not as retail-ready stock.
## The $282.8 million figure

The sheriff's valuation divides out to exactly $1,200 a pound. That is a flat street-value assumption applied to the full weight. The release does not explain how the rate was chosen or whether it distinguishes between finished and unfinished product.

For scale, California's licensed market recorded $987 million in sales in the third quarter of 2026, as we reported on 20 November. The value officials place on this one seizure is equal to about 29% of that quarter's legal sales. Even if the true market value is well below the official figure, the volume is the point: this was an industrial operation, not a grow house.
> When a site this size can call itself a hemp processor, the line between the two crops is doing more work than it can bear.
## Why the hemp label matters

Hemp and marijuana are the same plant, separated in law by THC content. That makes hemp a convenient cover. A warehouse full of green plant material looks the same either way until someone tests it, and hemp processors do not hold cannabis licences or report into the state's track-and-trace system.

The timing adds weight to the case. A stricter federal definition of hemp, based on total THC, is due to take effect on 11 December unless Congress changes it. Lawmakers pushing to replace the ban with regulation argue that licensing and testing would do more to police the sector than prohibition. Opponents of the hemp trade will point to Chico as evidence that the category is being abused. Both sides now have a 235,661-pound exhibit.

Licensed California operators have their own stake. They pay state excise tax and carry testing and compliance costs that an unlicensed processor does not. Product leaving a site like this one competes with theirs at a lower cost base. The California Statewide Law Enforcement Association, the union that represents state detectives including those at the Department of Cannabis Control, used the case to call for more state enforcement resources, arguing that illegal operations undercut licensed businesses and cost the state tax revenue.
## Not an isolated case

The Chico raid came eight days after another large operation. According to Hoodline, citing FOX40, a multi-agency effort led by the Sacramento County Sheriff's Office on 9 November searched 19 locations across California and Oregon, made eight arrests and seized or destroyed 30,000 pounds of illegal marijuana, along with 3,675 pounds of illegal pesticides. No source we reviewed links the two cases. By weight, Chico was nearly eight times larger.
## What we do not know

Who owned or leased the warehouses and who ran the operation has not been disclosed. It is not known whether any entity at the site held a hemp registration, where the plant material was grown, or where the finished product was headed. The role of the Bureau of Land Management suggests a link to cultivation on federal land, but officials have not said so. Charges, if any, have not been announced.
## What to watch

Watch for charging decisions from the Butte County District Attorney and for the first court dates of those arrested. Watch whether investigators name the business behind the site and whether it held any state hemp registration. Watch whether federal agencies bring a case of their own, given the Bureau of Land Management's part in the investigation. And watch 11 December: if the federal hemp definition takes effect as written, hemp-front operations lose a layer of legal cover, and regulators gain a simpler test.
